C0.quote: obviously strategy-proof and onto social choice functions on the domain
C0.note: Social choice functions (generalized median voter schemes) aggregating agents' single-peaked preferences over a public alternative; incentive properties (obvious strategy-proofness) of the procedure.

C1.quote: A generalized median voter scheme is obviously strategy-proof if and only if
C1.note: Main results characterise which rules satisfy obvious strategy-proofness (an incentive property); AX and SB fit equally well for the primary type, so the first listed (AX) is chosen. Theorem 2 constructs an extensive game form via an algorithm, but there is no complexity analysis, so AL is not coded.

C2.1.value: preference profile ("(preference) profile"; single-peaked preference profiles)

C2.2.quote: strict preference Pi (a linear order) over X:
C2.2.note: Strict single-peaked linear orders; the rules are tops-only but are defined on full profiles. In the extensive game forms agents choose actions in {x, x+1}, but the argument of the SCF is the preference profile.

C2.3.quote: where each i 2 N uses Pi to evaluate the outcomes
C2.3.note: Agents hold preferences Pi used to evaluate outcomes of strategy profiles, separately from the strategies/actions they choose.

C2.4.quote: action di¤erent from the one prescribed by i’s truth-telling strategy
C2.4.note: Strategy-proofness is defined with misreports Pi' distinct from the true Pi (Sec. 2, p. 7), and in the extensive game form behavioural strategies are separate notation from preferences, with a designated truth-telling strategy.

C3.1.note: Every main result (Theorems 1-2, Corollaries 1-3) concerns whether truth-telling is obviously dominant against all deviations.

C4.1.note: Input format is RANK but the paper uses none of utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost, distortion, intensity of preference.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences (or equivalent) is not used.

C5.1.loc: Checked: Abstract; Sec. 1 Introduction incl. literature review; Sec. 2 Preliminaries; Sec. 4-6; Sec. 7 Conclusion; Appendix
C5.1.note: Only mentions of efficiency are descriptions of other papers' results in other settings (literature review, p. 4); the paper's own results concern obvious strategy-proofness, ontoness and anonymity only.

VOT.quote_behav: agents are absolutely pessimistic when assessing the consequence of truth-telling
VOT.quote_info: the perfect information implies that all information sets are singleton sets
VOT.note: Agents (voters) choose strategies in an extensive game form; the analysis checks whether truth-telling is obviously dominant. Under perfect information they observe earlier actions of others; nothing is said about knowledge of others' preferences, and the dominance criterion evaluates worst/best cases over others' later actions.

CAN.note: Alternatives (e.g. public good levels, party platforms) are not modelled as agents.

DES.note: A designer is mentioned in passing in the literature comparison (p. 5), but the designer's choice or objective is not modelled.

C8.1.quote: implements it in obviously dominant strategies.
C8.1.note: Obvious dominance (Li 2017), i.e. truth-telling weakly dominant in a perfect-information extensive game form; also standard strategy-proofness.

C8.2.quote: implements it in obviously dominant strategies.

C9.1.note: Application examples in the introduction (public good levels, party platforms, room temperatures) only motivate the model; the conclusion's claims are about how restrictive obvious strategy-proofness is as a notion, not about real institutions, voters' well-being or which rule should be used. Borderline: the introduction mentions OSP mechanisms being 'easy to play', attributed to the literature.
